Empirical Research Plan  
“Medicare Spending, Physician Workforce, and the Quality of Care”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: 2-stage least squares (panel IV) with a Bartik / shift–share instrument, complemented by an event-study visualization of dynamic effects.

Why IV?  
•  Endogeneity: High-spending regions may have sicker beneficiaries; physician density may respond to demand shocks.  
•  Rich panel (regions × years, ≥10 yrs) allows fixed-effects to soak up time-invariant differences, but time-varying confounders remain.  
•  Policymakers periodically change Medicare payment formulas in ways that are national-level but interact with each region’s *predetermined* service mix or graduate-medical-education (GME) cap. These interactions supply quasi-random variation.

Instrument 1 (for spending) – “payment-mix Bartik”:  
PredictedSpending_r,t = Σ_s  (BaseShare_r,s,1995 × NationalFee_s,t)  
NationalFee_s,t = national year-t payment update for DRG / CPT group s.  
Intuition: When Congress raises the fee for cardiology services, regions that historically did a lot of cardiology (high BaseShare) receive a larger mechanical spending shock. BaseShares are fixed long before the outcomes we study.

Instrument 2 (for physician workforce) – “residency cap exposure”:  
PredictedPhysicians_r,t = 1996 Residents_r × NationalGMEExpansions_t / Population_r,1996  
1996 residents were frozen by the 1997 Balanced Budget Act; later modest policy-driven expansions were allocated proportional to the frozen caps. This yields plausibly exogenous changes in physician supply.

Dynamic event-study graphs (first-stage and reduced-form) will be used to demonstrate parallel pre-trends and temporal shape but will not constitute the main estimator.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variables  
T1_r,t  = log(Medicare spending per beneficiary)  
T2_r,t  = Physicians per 1,000 beneficiaries

Control (counterfactual)  
Regions whose predicted spending/physician supply changed little provide the comparison group; the fixed-effects IV uses all cross-regional differential exposure, so “controls” are implicitly low-exposure regions/years.

Timing  
Annual panel 1995–2015. National fee updates happen each January; we define treatment year t as fiscal year.

No running variable; not an RDD design.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: National fee/GME shocks strongly shift actual regional spending / workforce. Testable via first-stage F-statistics (>10).  
Plausibility: Prior literature (e.g., Clemens–Gottlieb 2014) finds F ≈ 50–200.

A2. Exclusion: National price shocks or GME quota changes affect quality *only through* their effect on spending/workforce, not through alternative channels.  
Plausibility: Shocks are nationwide and unrelated to local health shocks; service mix shares are predetermined. We will include region and year FE plus region-specific linear trends.

A3. Independence: Conditional on FE, the interaction of baseline shares with national shocks is as good as random.  
Plausibility enhanced by using 1995 baseline (pre-period) and controlling for observable baseline demographics and disease burden interacted with year.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): A shock to one region does not (materially) change quality in another through spillovers.  
Plausibility: Medicare patients seldom cross HRR boundaries for routine care; we test robustness excluding large spillover hubs (NYC, Boston).

A5. Monotonicity (IV): Regions more exposed to fee increases do not systematically cut spending. Obvious with positive price shocks.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Predetermined service mix may itself predict future health trends.  
•  Mitigation: (i) Control for baseline morbidity × year; (ii) show balanced pre-trends; (iii) conduct leave-one-out (“jackknife”) Bartik to minimize own-region mechanical correlation.

Threat 2: National policy changes may coincide with unrelated nationwide quality initiatives (e.g., Hospital Compare rollout).  
•  Mitigation: Include year FE, but also year × Census-division FE to absorb region-specific macro shocks; run placebo using privately insured patients (should not react to Medicare fees).

Threat 3: Measurement error in physician counts (especially small rural HRRs).  
•  Mitigation: Instrument alleviates attenuation; additionally, winsorize extremes and show robustness to alternative sources (AMA Masterfile vs. CMS physician compare).

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)          # high-dimensional IV
library(ggplot2)
library(ivpack)          # weak-ID diagnostics

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load Data
# -------------------------------------------------
spend   <- fread("medicare_spending.csv")      # HRR-year file
phys    <- fread("physician_counts.csv")
quality <- fread("quality_metrics.csv")
fees    <- fread("national_fee_updates.csv")   # DRG/CPT × year
share95 <- fread("baseline_service_mix_1995.csv")
gme     <- fread("gme_caps.csv")

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Merge and Construct Variables
# -------------------------------------------------
panel <- merge(spend, phys, by = c("hrr","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, quality, by = c("hrr","year"))

## 2a.  Bartik instrument for spending
# Expand to service-mix long form
long <- merge(share95, fees, by = "service")
long[, bartik := base_share * nat_fee]
iv_spend <- long[, .(Z_spend = sum(bartik)), by = .(hrr, year)]

## 2b.  Instrument for physician workforce
gme[, Z_phys := resid96 * nat_gme_expansion / pop96]
iv_phys <- gme[, .(hrr, year, Z_phys)]

panel <- merge(panel, iv_spend, by = c("hrr","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, iv_phys , by = c("hrr","year"))

# Outcomes
panel[, Q_mort := hosp_30day_mortality]
panel[, Q_readm := hosp_30day_readmit]

# Treatment vars
panel[, T_spend := log(med_spend_per_benef)]
panel[, T_phys  := phys_per_1000]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main Specification
# -------------------------------------------------
est_main <- feols(Q_mort ~ 1 | hrr + year  | 
                  T_spend ~ Z_spend , data = panel, cluster = "hrr")
summary(est_main)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Combined 2SLS with Both Endogenous Vars
# -------------------------------------------------
est_dual <- feols(Q_mort ~ 1 | hrr + year  | 
                  c(T_spend, T_phys) ~ c(Z_spend, Z_phys),
                  data = panel, cluster = "hrr")
summary(est_dual)

# Weak-ID test
ivreg_main <- ivreg(Q_mort ~ T_spend + factor(hrr) + factor(year) | 
                    Z_spend + factor(hrr) + factor(year), data = panel)
weakiv_test(ivreg_main, diagnostics = TRUE)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness: Leave-One-Out Bartik & Placebo
# -------------------------------------------------
## Leave-one-out instrument
long[, bartik_loo := (sum(nat_fee * base_share) - nat_fee*base_share) / 
                      (1 - base_share)]
iv_spend_loo <- long[, .(Z_spend_loo = sum(bartik_loo)), by = .(hrr, year)]
panel <- merge(panel, iv_spend_loo, by = c("hrr","year"), all.x = TRUE)

est_loo <- feols(Q_mort ~ 1 | hrr + year |
                 T_spend ~ Z_spend_loo, data = panel, cluster = "hrr")
summary(est_loo)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
•  Sign: I expect *negative* coefficients—higher spending and greater physician density improve quality (lower mortality/readmissions).  
•  Rough magnitude (mortality): A 10 percent rise in spending predicted to lower 30-day mortality by about 0.5–1.0 percentage points (elasticity ≈ –0.1). Physician workforce likely has a smaller but still negative effect (–0.3 pp per additional physician per 1,000).

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV method)
-------------------------------------------------
C1 (Relevance): 1  
C2 (Exclusion / no direct path): 0.5  
C3 (Independence from unobs. shocks): 0.5  
C4 (Monotonicity): 1  
C5 (SUTVA): 0.5  

Total = 3.5 / 5.
